items.desc: In some magnetic materials, the spins of individual atoms line up in highly ordered patterns but point in directions that almost completely cancel out, leaving the material unmagnetized. The exact arrangement of these spins can strongly affect how electrons move through a material, shaping both its electrical and magnetic properties. But because a single crystal can support such a huge number of plausible spin patterns, it would be impossible to test them one at a time.

items.title: How learning on the land is bringing back traditional food knowledge and healing
items.desc: A viral 2017 poll claimed that 7% of American adults believe chocolate milk comes from brown cows. The results drew a lot of laughs, along with criticism of the poll's accuracy. But nearly a decade later, the results still raise an important question: How much do people really know about where their food comes from and how it's grown?

items.title: Plant-inspired adhesive joins tiny blood vessels without stitches
items.desc: Sewing together a blood vessel just a millimeter wide is delicate work. The connection must withstand each pulse while limiting damage to the vessel's inner lining. A new adhesive inspired by plant roots offers another approach. In rats, it cut the average joining time from about 39 minutes to less than nine while preserving a smoother passage for blood.

items.title: Snapping shrimp without their 'helmets' show signs of disorientation after a blast from a nearby neighbor
items.desc: Snapping shrimp wield weapons powerful enough to endanger their own nervous systems. By quickly closing an oversized claw, they create a bubble whose collapse releases a shock wave. During fights, rivals can fire these blasts within a centimeter (0.4 inches) of each other's eyes and brains.

items.title: New agent framework facilitates biological database retrieval and integration
items.desc: Biological research questions often span multiple bioinformatics databases, which differ in data structures, access interfaces and coverage. To retrieve and integrate data across databases, researchers need to select suitable sources and call the corresponding query interfaces.

items.title: Seeds, preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests
items.desc: People may have been getting high off cannabis earlier than previously thought—at least 2,800 years ago, a new study suggests.

items.title: Why squeezing a rock can pull it apart
items.desc: When a brittle material, such as a ceramic, rock or concrete sample, is squeezed between two plates, it can split lengthwise, even if the plates are pushing its ends together. So far, the physical explanation for this phenomenon has remained largely unclear.

items.title: Researchers explore the use of AI and smart sensors to improve food safety quickly, affordably
items.desc: The smartJAN project, developed by the eVIDA research group at the University of Deusto in collaboration with Kernet and Fundación Miranda, has completed the development of a functional prototype capable of detecting the presence of LTPs (lipid transfer proteins), a family of plant proteins that includes allergens capable of triggering severe allergic reactions. These allergens are particularly relevant in the Mediterranean region.

items.title: Event Horizon Telescope views the dynamics and geometry of a black hole jet in extreme detail
items.desc: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), a massive international collaboration of scientists and radio observatories, is like the gift that keeps on giving. In 2019, the EHT Collaboration gave us the first image of a black hole: the supermassive black hole (SMBH) at the heart of the M87 galaxy (M87*). In 2022, it provided the first image of Sagittarius A*, the SMBH at the center of the Milky Way. Between 2024 and 2026, the international array also produced detailed images of the relativistic jets emanating from 3C 84 and M87*.

items.title: Should space data centers run on solar panels, nuclear reactors or both?
items.desc: The last few days we've been covering a series of papers by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory about the constraints surrounding the use of orbital data centers in space. One that has come up repeatedly is weight, and the solar panels used to power these data centers contribute a significant portion of that weight. So why not go with an alternative power source? Nuclear energy in space applications is having a bit of a moment currently—maybe it could provide the power needed for the orbital data center revolution?

items.title: New technologies help Natural History Museum uncover 92 species in its transformed gardens
items.desc: The Natural History Museum's transformed gardens in South Kensington are revealing new insights into London's urban wildlife. Among the 92 species recorded at the site for the first time between its reopening in July 2024 and the end of 2025 are the striking emperor moth and small red-eyed damselfly.

items.title: RNA discovery reveals how gut bacterium adapts to life in intestinal mucus
items.desc: The mucus layer in the human gut is a tough place for bacteria: nutrients are scarce, and conditions are harsh. How do bacteria adapt to such extreme environments? Researchers at the Helmholtz Institute for RNA-based Infection Research (HIRI) and the Chair of Microbiology of the Julius-Maximilians-Universität (JMU) in Würzburg, working with scientists at Vanderbilt Health in the United States, have identified a key regulator.

items.title: AI simulates electron hops over far longer times than conventional quantum calculations
items.desc: To predict how a material will behave, we need to know which atoms are located where. This allows us, for example, to explain whether a material is suitable as a catalyst for certain chemical reactions. But often, that is not enough: even if all the atoms stay exactly where they are, the distribution of electric charge within the material can change dramatically. Electrons can jump from one atom to another, changing the forces between atoms as well as the material's chemical reactivity.

items.title: Targeted conversion of carbon dioxide into chemical feedstocks: CO₂ helps shape its own catalyst
items.desc: Electrochemists at the University of Duisburg-Essen have discovered through computer simulations that carbon dioxide (CO₂) helps shape the surface of its own catalyst when the catalyst is restructured using voltage pulses. The calculations suggest that this allows CO₂ to be converted preferentially into formic acid. The findings have been published in Advanced Functional Materials.

items.title: Rocks under the lens: A simple microscope opens new possibilities for quantitative rock analysis
items.desc: Rocks hold a wealth of information about Earth's history. The size, shape and orientation of the mineral grains that make them up can reveal how rocks formed, deformed and changed deep beneath the surface. However, collecting this information has traditionally required specialized equipment and time-consuming analysis.

items.title: Yale scientists may have found a shortcut to the anti-aging benefits of eating less
items.desc: Yale researchers have discovered that moderate calorie restriction reduces an immune protein linked to aging and chronic inflammation, apparently independently of weight loss. Blocking this protein could potentially mimic some of the benefits of eating less and help people stay healthier for longer.

items.title: Facing extinction, the world’s largest sea turtle is making a surprising move
items.desc: The world’s largest sea turtle may be adapting to climate change by establishing new nesting grounds along Ecuador’s cooler coastline, where researchers have recorded unprecedented nesting activity and promising hatching rates. The discovery offers a rare glimmer of hope for a critically endangered population that has declined by more than 90% since the 1980s.

items.title: James Webb discovers a nearly pristine galaxy from 13 billion years ago
items.desc: Astronomers have discovered an extraordinarily primitive galaxy from 13 billion years ago that may carry the chemical fingerprints of the universe’s first stars. The discovery could solve a decades-old mystery surrounding ancient galaxies near the Milky Way and reveal how the building blocks of life first spread across the cosmos.

items.title: The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret
items.desc: The narwhal’s iconic spiral tusk, once prized in Europe as the horn of a mythical unicorn, conceals an extraordinary feat of natural engineering. Using advanced X-ray technology, an international team of scientists discovered that the tusk contains two intertwined microscopic spirals that twist in opposite directions.

items.title: Scientists turn one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance lubricating oil
items.desc: Virginia Tech scientists have discovered how to transform one of the world's hardest-to-recycle plastics into a valuable ingredient for high-performance engine oil. Their innovative process converts discarded PVC into a useful lubricant material in just three hours. The breakthrough could turn a major source of plastic pollution into a valuable industrial resource while making lubricant production more sustainable.

items.title: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time
items.desc: Scientists have identified two potentially critical periods when screen time may be especially detrimental to children's learning and memory: infancy and the start of formal schooling. Greater screen exposure during these developmental windows was linked to poorer academic performance and weaker working memory years later.

items.title: These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years
items.desc: Giant horned mammals that emerged shortly after the extinction of the dinosaurs may have had far fewer physical differences between males and females than scientists once believed. The discovery challenges a classic example of sexual dimorphism and raises questions about how historical biases have shaped our understanding of extinct animals.

items.title: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades
items.desc: A famous 345-million-year-old fossil has turned out to be something entirely different from what scientists believed for decades. Advanced X-ray imaging revealed hidden gills and thousands of tiny teeth, exposing a primitive aquatic or amphibious creature rather than an early reptile. The discovery suggests that several adaptations associated with life on land actually evolved in animals still dependent on water.

items.title: The surprising reason women seem better at multitasking than men
items.desc: Men and women appear to be similarly capable of multitasking, but men are more than twice as likely to ignore conversation while juggling multiple activities. Researchers believe this unexpected difference may help explain why women are widely perceived as better multitaskers.

items.title: For decades, scientists may have misunderstood how brain cells work
items.desc: A major new study challenges a long-standing assumption about how the brain works, revealing that most neurons are versatile multitaskers rather than highly specialized workers. By analyzing recordings from 43 regions of the mouse brain, researchers discovered that although some neurons are dedicated to specific functions, most respond to a wide variety of information in remarkably distinct ways.

items.title: Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea
items.desc: More than a mile beneath the surface of the Red Sea, scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes that could reveal secrets about Earth's ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life. Known as brine pools, these extremely salty, oxygen-free environments are surprisingly teeming with microbial life, challenging our understanding of where living organisms can survive.

items.title: Scientists discover signs of a hidden extinction crisis deep beneath the ocean
items.desc: The deep sea has long been considered a safe haven for marine life, but new genetic research suggests a hidden biodiversity crisis may be unfolding far beneath the waves. Scientists analyzing more than a decade of genetic data from five species of deep-sea fish and shrimp in the Gulf discovered troubling signs of extinction risk in every species examined.

items.title: Deep beneath Australia, hidden caves could unlock the secrets of alien worlds
items.desc: Scientists have solved the mystery of strange trenches scattered across Australia’s vast Nullarbor Plain, revealing an extensive hidden world beneath the surface. These subtle landscape features are created as deeply buried cave systems slowly collapse upward over millions of years. The discovery could help researchers locate unexplored caves containing ancient environmental records and unusual life forms.

items.title: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected
items.desc: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, despite being designed to study distant galaxies and the mysteries of the dark Universe. The icy object is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and follows an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.

items.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
items.desc: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.

items.title: Reimagining Food Innovation
items.desc: Some of the most significant innovations surrounding food are not high-tech scientific advances but low-tech social practices and relations, such as new ways of cooperating and distributing responsibility. To fix our broken food systems, we must demand that the best of these practices receive respect and investment.

items.title: Gun Buybacks Work, But Not the Way We Thought
items.desc: Some argue that gun buybacks are pointless unless they lower homicide rates. But new research into Mexico City’s gun-buyback program suggests that such measures can meaningfully reduce nonlethal injuries, which are more common than homicides, and can have serious psychological and other lasting health consequences.

items.title: The Future of the Global Disability Agenda
items.desc: The once-reasonable assumption that integrating disabled people into the existing multilateral order would help them benefit from the results being delivered no longer holds. Achieving better outcomes requires learning from disability movements about how to put diversity, access, care, and participation at the center of the agenda.

items.title: Can the AI Mineral Rush Advance a Just Green Transition?
items.desc: The scramble to secure huge amounts of copper, aluminum, lithium, cobalt, and other minerals for AI infrastructure risks undoing the progress made, as part of the green transition, toward more responsible mining practices. But it could also be an opportunity to support sustainable development in producer countries.

items.title: The Evolving Terrain of the Global AI Transformation
items.desc: The race to build ever more powerful AI models is heating up, but so far there is little evidence of the promised productivity surge. Whether that changes will depend on how quickly employers adopt AI and whether governments can encourage its use while managing the risks of job losses and public backlash.

items.title: How Congress Can Give Americans What They Want
items.desc: American households are footing the bill for President Donald Trump’s tariffs and war in Iran through higher prices and borrowing costs. Congress has the power to stop this by reclaiming its authority over tariff policy and the use of military force, and by requiring a public accounting of the costs of future wars.

items.title: The Revolt Against Oligarchy
items.desc: The extraordinary power wielded by today’s billionaires is a threat to democracy and the planet. Encouragingly, people around the world, frustrated by a lack of affordability and worsening job prospects, are beginning to discover just how much political power they can wield.

items.title: Who Can Speak for Europe in Peace Talks with Russia?
items.desc: The European Union's inability to find one person to represent it in such negotiations reflects a structural failure, not a shortage of skilled personnel. That is why the EU should step aside and delegate the selection of an envoy to the United Kingdom, France, and Germany.

items.title: The Fossil-Fuel Endgame Doesn’t Require a COP Consensus
items.desc: Despite the failure of this year's United Nations climate talks, there is no doubt that phasing out fossil fuels is the right goal. The only question is whether a coalition of the willing can use policy to push markets toward a faster, fairer, and smoother transition than the traditional COP process can deliver.

items.title: Who Controls America’s AI Chokepoint?
items.desc: The saga of Jensen Huang's ouster and sudden return as Nvidia's chief executive has exposed a paradox at the heart of American technological hegemony. While Nvidia's AI chips give the United States leverage over China, the geopolitical power that Nvidia makes possible gives it leverage over the US.

items.title: Where Development Cooperation Still Lives
items.desc: By helping developing economies build the capacity and infrastructure trade requires, the World Trade Organization's Aid for Trade initiative has contributed to a significant increase in these countries' share of global exports over the past 20 years. But the trade landscape is changing fast, and Aid for Trade must adapt.

items.title: Nvidia’s Liability Problem Isn’t Going Away
items.desc: Given previous suspicions about Nvidia's engagement with China, one wonders if Jensen Huang’s admitted extramarital affairs are just a cover-up for more consequential violations and misrepresentations. Whatever the case, the problem is not limited to Huang; with his reinstatement as CEO, it involves the company's entire board.

items.title: Mapping Strategic Supply-Chain Risk
items.desc: If there is a premium to be paid for resilient supply chains, who will foot the bill? The answer can be found through a three-stage approach of identifying current vulnerabilities, letting markets and public tenders price them, and then having national-security authorities intervene only where market pricing fails.

Here, we present a selection of recent works by PS contributors that are worth adding to your holiday shopping list (and your bookshelf).

This is in line with daily news stories on the “vulnpocalypse” and “Black October.” Surprisingly though, data on real-world impacts of cyber attacks tells a less dire story. If this trend continues, it could indicate that attribution and punishment matter at least as much as attackers’ technical capabilities.
